In an attempt to reduce fraud in Brazil's "antiquated land titling system,"9 which enables swathes of Amazon rainforest to be cut down for soy and beef farming, and in a country where half the population lack property rights, blockchain has been identified as a possible solution by both local and national Brazilian governments.

Due to there being no single, centralized system for checking who owns land in Brazil, and instead, registration in different regions is done by "one of some 3,400 privately-owned agents, known as cartorios,"10 the Brazilian municipalities of Pelotas and Morro Redondo's Real Estate Registry Offices have partnered with Ubitquity to address the issue of corruption in land ownership dealings.
Ubitquity is a U.S.-based blockchain company "offering a simple user experience for securely recording and tracking property deeds."11
Serpro is the largest government-owned corporation of IT services in Brazil. It was created on December 1, 1964 to modernize and give agility to strategic sectors of public administration.12

The current system in Brazilian land registry is "confusing and widely abused, with double allocations and corruption in the maintenance of records and transfer of title deeds fueling land conflicts."13

President Kersti Kaljulaid stated during a visit to the Atlantic Council, an American think-tank in international affairs, that "the government is currently piloting a blockchain application related to traffic accident reporting. With Blockchain the entire case could be handled in 30 minutes."23
The Estonian solution is described as "simple, elegant and secure."24

e-Estonia, in describing their system, states that the "unique aspect of e-Estonia is that it lacks a centralized or master database – all information is held in a distributed data system and can be exchanged instantly upon request, providing access 24/7."25
Estonia is extremely proud of their e-Estonia initiative, with the e-Estonia website listing all initiatives as "success stories."26

During a signing ceremony at the Ministry of Justice in April 2016, Papuna Ugrekhelidze, chairman of the Republic of Georgia's National Agency of Public Registry (NAPR), which is a part of the Georgian Ministry of Justice, announced the Republic's mission to build a "blockchain-based property registry"27.

Chairman Papuna Ugrekhelidze outlined three reasons why Georgia was seeking out blockchain as a solution to land registry issues. He states "first, [blockchain] will add security to the data (property registration) so the data cannot be corrupted. Second, by powering the registry with the blockchain, public auditors will also be able to make real-time audits. So, the auditor will audit the registry not once per year, but every 10 minutes (for example). Third, it will reduce the friction in registration and the cost of property rights registration, because people could do this in the future using their smart phones."28
He concludes his remarks by stating that "blockchain will be used as a notary service."29

During the same ceremony, Valery Vavilov, CEO of the developing company, also stated that BitFury was at that time in the process of developing a property rights registration project for Georgian citizens, to provide the opportunity to register property on the blockchain.30

BitFury CEO Valery Vavilov explained that all the changes were made on the back end and the only dichotomy for the citizens of Georgia "is that they can monitor if a title is legitimate when it is entered into the system."31
According to BitFury, the platform will utilize a permissioned blockchain operated by the NAPR. This private blockchain will be tied to the bitcoin blockchain.32
The system was designed to boost land title transparency, reduce the prevalence of fraud, and bring significant time and cost savings in the registration process.33
In 2017, BitFury CEO Valery Vavilov, shared with the media that the Georgian government was "excited about how the whole work was handled and executed with the current method."34

At the time of the April 2016 ceremony, according to BitFury, a custom-designed blockchain system had already been integrated into the digital records system of the National Agency of Public Registry (NAPR), though not yet made active.35

On April 19th, 2017, Valery Vavilov, CEO of BitFury, during his speech at the Russian Internet Forum in Moscow, said, "since the launch in February 2017, [his] company along with the government of the Republic of Georgia had since implemented the property registration on Blockchain and had registered more than 100,000 documents."36

Reports indicate that the economic benefits of harnessing blockchain technology can amount to several million US-Dollars in the Jordanian refugee camp populations, alone.40
Building Blocks has integrated with an existing biometric authentication technology company, IrisGuard, to allow refugees to identify themselves "with the blink of an eye."41

When an individual then visits, for example, a supermarket wired to IrisGuard's "Eye Pay," at the checkout instead of handing over cash they look into the biometric scanner, which checks the blockchain database to both confirm their identity and the credit in their bank account.42

According to Ripple, this will allow Saudi banks to make faster, cheaper and more transparent cross-border transactions.45

Speaking broadly on blockchain as a financial technology (fintech), Ziad AlYousef, General Manager of Payment Systems at SAMA, stated "[SAMA's] first step is to increase the awareness and understanding of [blockchain] technologies among the banking, governmental and financial sector as well as educational sector in addition to creating awareness on the user side. [SAMA] wants to help [users] understand how they will have more efficient cost-effective services with these new technologies."46
The Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority will utilize xCurrent in facilitating payments between users.47
Ripple's operating platform, xCurrent, is an open-source technology built on the core principles of blockchain.48

RippleNet (Ripple) is a decentralized network based on an agreement between Ripple and network participants, such as SAMA, -- all of which utilize the same technology and adhere to a consistent set of payment rules and standards. Since 2015, Ripple and an advisory team made up of a diverse set of leading transaction bankers inlcuding Bank of America, Santander, and Westpac. RippleNet has been building the "Rulebook," a common framework that ensures operational consistency and legal clarity for every transaction. This group actively advises on maintaining and enhancing the rules and standards as RippleNet grows.49

AlYousef maintains that SAMA remains committed to developing blockchain based applications in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's financial sector. AlYousef adds that blockchain technology needs regulations and legislations, and that this is the role SAMA plays today and will continue to play in the future.50

Next, interested investors buy in to the offering, either with fiat currency (traditional money as prescribed by a government) or with preexisting digital tokens such as [Bitcoin]. In exchange for their support, investors receive a new cryptocurrency token specific to the ICO."9 ICOs can be considered problematic by governments due to the facts that first, ICOs are decentralized, with no single authority governing them, and second, ICOs are largely unregulated, meaning that government organizations do not oversee them.10 This allows for the possibility of illicit trades and other activities that may challenge the rule of law. ICOs also come with the risk of fraudulent offerings that prey on unwitting investors.

While Australia has historically taken an open stance with cryptocurrencies, in the wake of the August 2017 "financial scandal surrounding the Commonwealth Bank of Australia, the Australian government sought to follow in Japan's footsteps by strengthening its anti-money laundering laws and regulating digital currencies. This differed slightly from the view in 2015 that the Australian government would seek a "hands-off" approach to cryptocurrencies. Still, the lack of more concise regulation has purportedly had a negative impact on the country as the end of 2017 saw Australian cryptocurrency brokers halt Australian dollar deposits."11 December 2017 also saw an issuance from the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) which hinted at the way potential future regulation could go.

In December of 2017, the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) became the first major stock market to announce the adoption of blockchain technology to record shareholdings and manage the clearing and settlement of equity transactions.12

A decentralized economic system, one that in essence takes power away from the central government, is antithetical to the very doctrine of the Chinese Communist Party, the ruling political party of the People's Republic of China, and the party of Xi Jinping, China's recently confirmed "President for Life."14

In late 2013, China's Central Bank (the People's Bank of China) barred financial institutions from partaking in digital currency and Bitcoin transactions, but individuals were free to trade as they wished.17
By early 2017, Chinese bitcoin miners (individuals or groups who create the digital currency by solving complex algorithms) made up over fifty percent of the worldwide mining population.18

It came as a shock to many in the cryptocurrency world when, in late 2017, the Peoples Bank of China (PBC) adopted a strong stance against the mining and trading of cryptocurrencies in mainland China.19
In mid-2018, China took steps to shut down blockchain news accounts, ban ICOs20, and ban hotels in Beijing from hosting cryptocurrency events, among other such measures.21
In mid-2018, China took steps to shut down blockchain news accounts, ban ICOs20, and ban hotels in Beijing from hosting cryptocurrency events, among other such measures.21

According to sources familiar with the matter, there have been no explicit explanations for the Chinese crackdown on the cryptocurrency market. However, cleansing risk from financial markets has been a government mantra for more than two years.22

Furthermore, among the main concerns is that digital currencies also provide a way to move money out of China, potentially adding to outflows that officials have aggressively set about stemming. Mark McFarland, chief economist at Union Bancaire Privee SA HK, said the clampdown moves "suggest a longer term process of tightening scrutiny of activities that aren't in the normal sort of monetary realm."23

Bloomberg adequately sums up the state of affairs in stating that "China's vision [seems] to be based more on taking full control of such transactions in contrast to the libertarian aspirations of Bitcoin."24

Frank Schaeffler, a member of the German parliament's Finance Committee, who pushed for legal classification of bitcoins stated in 2013 that "[Germany] should have competition in the production of money. I have long been a proponent of Friedrich August von Hayek's scheme to denationalize money. Bitcoins are a first step in this direction."25
In early 2017, reports indicated that the International Monetary Fund was "exploring using blockchain technology for its own trading of special drawing rights."26

Later that year, in June of 2017, the IMF released a forty-nine page Staff Discussion Note in which they discuss the potential future for blockchain and cryptocurrencies in today's financial systems.27

The Note focuses on cryptocurrencies in stating that "in their current form, virtual currencies are not likely to be adequate stores of value given the volatility in their exchange rates to fiat money. This same volatility would undermine hub-and-spoke networks, as two 'foreign exchange rate' conversions are needed: when the token is acquired, and when it is sold. Even if the virtual currency is held for very short periods, the transaction involves foreign exchange rate risk. FX risk could potentially be hedged, although costs could then rival those of correspondent bank transfers.'"28

The note then goes on to state, in seeming support of cryptocurrencies, that: "DLT-based Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) could also be more secure and resilient than current settlement systems which are exposed to single point of failure risk. Finally, by facilitating small value payments, it could boost the adoption and efficiency of the new, decentralized, service economy. However, CBDCs raise multiple potential costs and risks, such as managing the platform and its integrity, resolving scalability, and dealing with issues of privacy."29

In November of 2017, Japan held the title of the largest Bitcoin market in the world. Since then, Japan has fallen behind only one country, the U.S., to currently hold the second place position at approximately 400,000 BTC traded for Japanese Yen at the time of this report, accounting for about 41% of the market.30
The Korean Won, Euro, and British Pound follow in third, fourth and fifth places respectively for a total of just 8% of the BTC market.31
Japan has been known by prominent enthusiasts of cryptocurrencies to have been an early supporter of the technology.32

This belief was validated on August 23, 2018 with a statement by Toshihide Endo, the newly appointed commissioner of Japan's Financial Services Agency (FSA), during which Mr. Endo states that Japan has "no intention to curb (the crypto industry) excessively."33

Following an early 2018 $530M crypto theft from a Japan based bitcoin wallet and exchange headquartered in Tokyo, the authority (FSA) revealed that it was "considering regulating crypto exchanges under the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (FIEA), instead of their current legal foundation, the Payment Services Act, to bolster consumer protection."34

Efforts to ensure the best possible future for Cryptocurrencies in Japan are being spearheded by what is described as a "self-regulating body put together in March (of 2018) [that] has been working towards keeping exchanges in line with the FSA's requirements for know your customer (KYC) and security rules. The Japan Virtual Currency Exchange Association (JVCEA), which is a voluntary organization, has also offered suggestions to the FSA about mandatory storage protocols as well as ways to keep all exchanges in line with the greater digital assets market."35

The Taskforce agreed upon objectives included "exploring the impact of cryptoassets, the potential benefits and challenges of the application of distributed ledger technology in financial services, and assessing what, if any, regulation is required in response."36

Andrew Bailey, Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Chief Executive stated during the May 2018 meeting: "Cryptoassets have been an area of increasing interest for markets and regulators globally including the FCA. [FCA] looks forward to working with our counterparts at the Bank of England and the Treasury as part of the taskforce to develop thinking and policy on cryptoassets."37

citations.citation_sentence: Such an approach provides developers the flexibility to innovate, including the ability to innovate in the actual controls, technical tools and safeguards, while maintaining consistency with core principles and outcomes.vi
citations.citation_footnote: There are no universally accepted definitions for AI developers, deployers, and users; indeed, a 2023 taxonomy jointly developed by the EU and U.S. described the definitions of deployment, developer, and user as "pending" (See "EU-U.S. Terminology and Taxonomy for Artificial Intelligence: First Edition", https://www.nist.gov/system/files/documents/noindex/2023/05/31/WG1%20AI%20Taxonomy%20and%20Terminology%20Subgroup%20List%20of%20Terms.pdf minology%20Subgroup%20List%20of%20Terms.pdf). In this paper, we use the term "developers" to refer to parties that design and build AI systems, "deployers" as parties that make such systems available for use, and "users" as the end-users that operate those systems on an ongoing basis.
